noticias.titulo: Myanmar faces historic genocide verdict at UN court over Rohingya massacres
noticias.resumen: No state has ever been found guilty by an international court of committing genocide.
noticias.texto:
Myanmar faces historic genocide verdict at UN court over Rohingya massacres
- Published
When the judges of the International Court of Justice read out their verdict in the seven-year-old genocide case filed by The Gambia against Myanmar on Thursday, they could make history.
In the years since the Genocide Convention was signed in 1948, after the Nazi Holocaust, dozens of individuals have been successfully prosecuted for the crime of genocide, in conflicts such as those in Rwanda and the former Yugoslavia.
But no state has ever been found guilty by an international court of committing genocide.
"It would be a judgment of landmark importance if The Gambia were to win this case," says Arsalan Suleman, the lawyer leading the case against Myanmar at the court. "It would give renewed vitality to the 1948 Genocide Convention and to the notion of international legal accountability for crimes committed by a state."
The mass expulsion of the Rohingya population of Rakhine State in August and September 2017 was without question a military operation of exceptional brutality.
I was among a very small number of journalists who witnessed the deliberate burning of Rohingya villages in Rakhine, and also the dreadful human suffering of the hundreds of thousands who fled to neighbouring Bangladesh.
Their accounts of killing, torture and mass rape by Burmese soldiers have been thoroughly documented by human rights groups and a United Nations fact-finding mission, external.
I have on many occasions interviewed ethnic Rakhine people about their animosity towards the Muslim population, and I have documented the systematic obliteration of what remained of Rohingya villages by the Myanmar state.
But the question posed at the UN's top court, the ICJ, is whether all of this amounted to genocide.
The ICJ was established in 1945 to help settle disputes between states, not to try international crimes. However, it was chosen to address the attacks on Rohingyas in Myanmar because there were few other avenues of redress for the victims.
Myanmar authorities have denied accusations of ethnic cleansing or genocide, saying they were only responding to terrorist actions by Rohingya militants with so-called military "clearance operations".
A UN report in 2018, based on hundreds of interviews, said the army's tactics were "grossly disproportionate to actual security threats". It said top military figures in Myanmar must be investigated for genocide in Rakhine State and crimes against humanity in other areas. Myanmar rejected the report.
As Myanmar was not a signatory to the International Criminal Court, it was not possible to file a case there against the officials accused of atrocities in Rakhine State.
Instead in November 2019 The Gambia, backed by the Organisation of Islamic Co-operation, filed a case at the ICJ, arguing that all states are bound by the Genocide Convention, so all have an interest in upholding it.
It accused the state in Myanmar, not just the military, of genocide.
This was a novelty in international law; a state not directly affected by an act, arguing that it had legal standing to make a complaint because it was indirectly affected by any violations of such an important convention.
Myanmar objected to this argument, but the ICJ judges ruled that The Gambia was eligible to file the case.
The case drew even more attention when the Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi, who at the time headed the elected government in Myanmar, chose to lead the initial legal defence of her country at The Hague in person, for which she was widely criticised.
She had very limited influence over the actions of the Myanmar military in Rakhine State, but her refusal to condemn them dismayed many of those who until then had admired her courage and adherence to democratic principles.
Since she was deposed by a coup in 2021 and placed under arrest the defence has been led by a new team appointed by the military.
Historically, proving that genocide has been committed has been very difficult. Judges apply a high bar to this.
Typically, where there is no explicitly genocidal programme, like that of the Nazis, the judges require that the evidence presented at court must be such that the only reasonable inference from the actions of the defendants is that they had genocidal intent.
When Bosnia-Herzegovina filed a genocide case against Serbia at the ICJ in 1993, it took the court 14 years to conclude that while incidents like the 1995 massacre at Srebrenica did amount to genocide, there was not sufficient proof that the state of Serbia had genocidal intent, though it was found to have failed to prevent genocide.
Myanmar's lawyers and Aung San Suu Kyi have argued something similar.
Suu Kyi said that The Gambia's team mischaracterised a complex conflict and military operation, and that while she accepted that war crimes may have been committed against the Rohingyas, that is not proof of genocidal intent.
But Arsalan Suleman believes the weight of evidence his team gathered is enough to meet that high bar.
"What we presented to the court was the long history of discrimination targeting the Rohingya, and how that history, and the policies connected with it, provide a background to understand the government's language, rhetoric, propaganda, and policies that were part of the 2017 'clearance operations'," Suleman said.
"We discussed the 1982 citizenship law, and the tightening noose of discriminatory laws that restricted access to education, healthcare, livelihoods, and travel - all of which made life really impossible for the Rohingya and, we argued, was one of several indicators of genocidal intent."
What happens if the court does find in favour of The Gambia?
Myanmar would then find itself tarnished by having committed "the crime of crimes", as sitting on the same bench as Nazi Germany, the Rwandan Hutu militants and the Bosnian Serbs at Srebrenica.
That might seem a setback for Min Aung Hlaing, the general who now runs Myanmar, who above all was responsible for the military's operations in 2017, and who has been trying to improve his dismal international image in recent months.
There is no right of appeal against an ICJ verdict. However, there is also no penalty that follows an ICJ verdict.
The Burmese coup leader is focused mostly on rebuilding relations with neighbouring Asian countries, who are unlikely to pay too much attention to such a verdict, and much less on rebuilding relations with Western countries who do care.
But for the huge Rohingya diaspora this verdict matters a great deal.
"This is like formal recognition of our suffering," says Mohammed Nowkim, a Rohingya who was driven out of the Rakhine town of Buthidaung in 2017 and now lives in Canada.
"For the Rohingya, this trial is a moment of acknowledgement of our suffering after years of denial. The Rohingya have been waiting for justice for decades, not just this year."
He and other Rohingya activists hope that a ruling in favour of The Gambia will prompt more co-ordinated action by other countries to find a resolution which allows them to go home to Rakhine State, in safety.
More than a million are stuck in wretched camps in Bangladesh, barred from employment as international funding dries up.
But the obstacles to realising this hope are formidable.
Rakhine State has been ravaged by a conflict between the military and the insurgent Arakan Army, which now controls most of the territory. It is supported by the indigenous Rakhine population who are very hostile to the idea of the Rohingyas coming back.
Many Rohingya villages have been completely destroyed. And international support for them has faded over the years. Even an unprecedented genocide verdict at the world's highest court cannot change that reality.

  - Published11 September 2017

noticias.titulo: Claude-maker Anthropic poised for stock market debut worth up to $1.5tn
noticias.resumen: Anthropic started just five years ago an is now one of the biggest names in artificial intelligence.
noticias.texto:
Claude-maker Anthropic poised for stock market debut worth up to $1.5tn
- Published
Anthropic is poised to hit a value of up to $1.5tn (Â£1.14tn) when its shares start trading on the stock market on Thursday.
The artificial intelligence (AI) company behind the popular chatbot Claude said its shares will be priced at $83 each when it lists on the Nasdaq, a tech-focused stock exchange based in New York.
That price will make it one of the most highly valued companies in the world.
It will be the first US firm focused exclusively on AI to go public, marking a crucial test for the fast-growing industry, which faces questions over whether the huge investment poured into the technology will be profitable.
The AI firm said earlier this month it would likely offer its shares for between $70 and $78 each, which valued the company at up to $1.3tn.
But demand for Anthropic's stock debut - commonly referred to as its initial public offering, or IPO - is very high, according to one early investor in the company who spoke with the BBC on condition of anonymity.
The person said shares were more than 10 times oversubscribed ahead of the public listing, meaning demand for Anthropic shares exceeded the number of shares available.
If that turns out to be the case, Anthropic's valuation could quickly blow past its target on Thursday when trading begins.
Crucial test for AI
Depending on how strong that demand is, Anthropic could even exceed the early market valuation of Elon Musk's SpaceX, which was the world's most highly valued stock debut when it went public with a value of $2.2tn in June.
However, in the weeks that followed, SpaceX shares fell significantly in price.
As it stands, Anthropic's listing will see the firm raise more than $68bn from its initial investors. It is also expecting another $26bn from private placements. So the total amount the company will raise is expected to be $94bn.
The amount of cash Anthropic has raised from its listing is already more than SpaceX raised in June.
OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT and Anthropic's biggest AI rival, is expected to go public next year.
Until then, Anthropic will be the only public company in the US that is entirely focused on the technology, or one that was founded and built around AI tools and products. Its scope is different from tech giants like Google and Microsoft that also develop AI but are involved in other tech services.
- The seven Anthropic founders who are about to become multi-billionaires 
  - Published2 hours ago
There is excitement around Anthropic's listing, but also some concern from investors around its ability to generate revenue and profits going forward.
Yang Wang, a principle financial analyst with Counterpoint Research, said the central issue for Anthropic is whether its business "can keep pace" as hundreds of billions of dollars in financial obligations come due in the next couple of years.
"Nevertheless, it is not an everyday occurrence for public investors to gain direct exposure to a frontier-model developer with the potential to shape the next stage of productivity," Wang said.
While nearly every other major tech company is pouring huge amounts of money into the technology and infrastructure required for their own AI tools, they are built around social media or online retail or online search. AI tools and applications are secondary.
"Anthropic going public gives us a whole new window into what AI demand looks like," Marta Norton, who heads strategy at investment firm Empower, told the BBC.
Rapid rise
Anthropic was started by a group of co-founders, led by siblings Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei, all of whom left their work at OpenAI to start a new AI firm.
The company has carved itself out in the ongoing AI race as more focused on building the technology with safety top of mind.
It refused to comply with a demand by the US Department of Defense that Anthropic's tools be used in an essentially unrestricted way.
CEO Dario Amodei has been outspoken in his belief that AI tools may soon be so powerful that they present a threat to human existence.
The company has urged developers to slow the development of AI, arguing that advanced systems could pose "catastrophic" risks to humanity if they are not handled with appropriate safeguards.
Rival firm OpenAI has also voiced similar concerns about the technology's risks and delayed its plans to list on the stock market to address AI safety concerns.
Nonetheless, Anthropic is looking to grow quickly and gain more access to financing through the public markets in order to do so.
Norton said Anthropic going public now, in a time of market volatility comes down to the simple fact that the company needs access to more money.
"AI is financially demanding," Norton said. "The public markets open up the financial spigot a little bit more, and so the time has come."
But broader anxieties have started to grow about the AI industry's business model, which is reliant on expensive computer chips that are in short supply. The technology is also dependent on controversial data centres and funding such operations require deals with other tech companies.
The Federal Reserve Bank has expressed concern about the rapid growth of AI-related debt being financed through "complex and opaque" structures, according to minutes from its October meeting to discuss a potential rate rise.
A few of the meeting's participants also noted that "AI-related exposures were becoming increasingly concentrated among a small number of firms".
With additional reporting by Rachel Clun and Osmond Chia

noticias.titulo: Van Gogh painting sells for record $190.4m after row over its Nazi history
noticias.resumen: Châtaigniers en fleurs was painted in 1890 in the final two months of Vincent van Gogh's life.
noticias.texto:
Van Gogh painting sells for record $190.4m after row over its Nazi history
- Published
Auction house Sotheby's has sold a painting by Vincent van Gogh for a record $190.4m (Â£144.8m).
The sale of ChÃ¢taigniers en fleurs ("Chestnut Trees in Blossom") shatters the renowned artist's previous auction record of $117.2 million set in 2022.
The historic sale in New York on Wednesday comes after an eleventh-hour agreement was reached to resolve a dispute regarding claims the art piece was previously sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.
ChÃ¢taigniers en fleurs was painted in 1890 in the final two months of Van Gogh's life. It is considered one of the most important works of art from that period to remain in private hands, according to Sotheby's.
It was not immediately clear who purchased the painting. The BBC has contacted Sotheby's for comment.
The oil painting, which was estimated to carry a value of $180m (Â£136m) prior to the sale, was put up for auction as part of a set called the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection.
Sotheby's announced in the hours before the auction that it had resolved a dispute between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and the heirs of the Fischer family - the prior German owners of the work - regarding the sale.
Representatives acting for heirs of the Fischer family had claimed the painting may have been sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.
A lawyer for the family's heirs reportedly wrote to Sotheby's on their behalf, telling the auction house that the painting was sold in Amsterdam before World War Two because of financial losses the Fischer family's publishing company suffered under the Nazis. The BBC has contacted the lawyer for comment.
"In recognition of the painting's complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution and the work will be sold pursuant to their agreement," Sotheby's said on Wednesday.
Sotheby's website details the provenance of the oil painting and how it has researched the artwork changing hands since 1890.
It says Samuel Fischer - a famous German publisher - acquired it 1909 before it was passed down in his family after his death in 1934.
The painting was deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933 before it went to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris in 1936, Sotheby's said.
Four other owners then had the painting.
The Blaquier family acquired it in 1975 and owned it for more than half a century before the latest sale, the auction house said.

noticias.titulo: Elon Musk says record spending on US midterms was 'pretty foolish'
noticias.resumen: The multi-billionaire also said he was "not Maga", distancing himself from the political movement linked to Trump.
noticias.texto:
Elon Musk says record spending on US midterms was 'pretty foolish'
- Published
Elon Musk said on Wednesday that he felt "pretty foolish" about the record sum he spent on the US midterm elections, following sweeping Republican defeats.
The Tesla and SpaceX CEO was the campaign's top individual donor, giving $446m (Â£339m) to support President Donald Trump's party, particularly in Texas where many of Musk's firms are based.
Musk, who had backed Trump's second White House bid, also said he was "not Maga" - the Make America Great Again movement associated with the president.
Democrats won control of the Senate and House, while Texas, Ohio and other states swung away from Trump, who has faced pressure over the impact his policies have had on the cost of living.
Musk was speaking virtually at the New York Times DealBook Summit, an annual conference hosted in the city attended by major business and political leaders.
"I'm not Maga," Musk said, referring to the right-wing political movement.
He added: "I'm not sure what Maga means... if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that."
Musk went on to say he did not see much for the money he had spent on the Republicans' campaign, though he added that it was likely that candidates would have fared worse without the spending.
One of the most striking midterms wins went to Democrat James Talarico, who beat Republican Ken Paxton for a US Senate seat in Texas.
According to BBC analysis, Musk had spent at least $45m in support of Paxton.
Texas is where key operations for Musk's car company Tesla and rocket and technology firm SpaceX are based.
Democrats have vowed greater scrutiny of tech companies, including over the roll out of controversial data centres.

noticias.titulo: Crimean Bridge attacked again, Russian official says
noticias.resumen: The head of Crimea said traffic was suspended after another attack on the link between Russia and the occupied territory.
noticias.texto:
Crimean Bridge attacked again, Russian official says
- Published
The Crimean Bridge has been attacked by Ukraine for the third time this week, a Russian official has said.
The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed that traffic was temporarily suspended following another strike on the bridge connecting Russia to occupied Crimea.
The critical bridge had already been hit twice earlier in the week resulting in severe damage and part of the bridge collapsing into the water.
The important infrastructure has long been targeted by Ukraine because of its significance as a logistical and symbolic asset to Moscow's war effort.
It comes as Russian President Vladimir Putin meets US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping on Thursday for landmark talks in China.
Aksyonov confirmed the strike on the bridge in the early hours of Thursday via Telegram, adding that assessment of the damage was under way.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian sources have continued to issue air raid alert warnings overnight for districts just outside of the capital Kyiv.
At least three people were killed in a Russian drone attack on Odesa on Wednesday, according to the regional state administration. Officials described the attack as "brutal and deliberate... directly targeting people and their lives".
President Volodymyr Zelensky has called the initial strikes on the Crimean Bridge as an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
Ukraine used drones and missiles against it on 17 November which brought down a key section of the road.
That section of the double-arched, 12-mile bridge now lies on the seabed, brought down by an arsenal of Ukrainian long-range weaponry in a seven-stage operation culminating in a dramatic collapse.
In response, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before".
While Ukrainian forces have struggled to close the bridge for good, recent attempts have brought them closer to destroying the bridge's crucial road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line.
Russian forces have also targeted key bridge crossings over the Dnipro River in Kyiv in recent days.
Russian strikes hit the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges causing traffic closures, partial damage to the metro system and some power and water outages.
  - Published1 day ago

noticias.titulo: Russian arrested for spying on US defence company Palantir over Ukraine support
noticias.resumen: The suspect followed employees and was found with fake US IDs and two Russian passports, prosecutors say.
noticias.texto:
Russian arrested for spying on US defence company Palantir over Ukraine support
- Published
A Russian man has been arrested in California's Silicon Valley for allegedly attempting to spy on employees of a technology and defence firm that supports the Ukrainian military.
Igor D'iu is accused of acting as an agent of a foreign government to conduct a covert operation in Palo Alto, near San Francisco. The BBC understands that the company targeted was Palantir Technologies.
D'iu is also charged with stalking employees and possessing falsified identity documents.
The company is not named in charging documents, but is described as a publicly traded technology and defence company that produces software used by Ukraine in its war with Russia.
"The allegations in this case describe a state-sponsored operation to target and harass employees of an American technology and defense company because of that company's assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia," said US Attorney for the Northern District of California Craig Missakian.
"We will not tolerate any efforts - by foreign governments or otherwise - to turn Silicon Valley into a base for foreign intelligence operations."
Prosecutors say that D'iu entered the US unlawfully via the Mexico border, after travelling there from Istanbul in June.
He was allegedly recruited through the Telegram encrypted messaging app. His handlers referred to Russia as "'the Motherland' and directed D'iu to gather information about the company because it was supplying weapons used against Russia in Ukraine".
On their instruction, he purchased computers, phones, wireless networking equipment and remote access software - tools he needed for his spy mission.
He then went to a coffee shop located near the company's offices in Palo Alto, where he photographed laptop screens of employees who were working there.
His handlers also allegedly "instructed him to position his laptop at designated locations near the company so they could remotely access it and attempt to collect information from company employees in the vicinity".
A source in the industry confirmed that Palantir was targeted, and added that the operation did not penetrate the company's private systems.
They added that the company has been "targeted extensively" by Russia over its involvement in Ukraine, and that the attacks are becoming "increasingly aggressive".
The source, who did not want to be named, said that this was the first time a Russian operative was found while on US soil attempting to spy on the company.
"I think the surprising thing is that they decided to take the risk of sending someone to the US," they said, in an attempt to get into the system "physically".
Palantir has not issued a statement in reaction to the charges.
D'iu also allegedly conducted surveillance of employees and their residences.
On 3 September, he followed a vehicle driven by one senior executive for nearly 30 miles. He fled after she drove to a police station. Police later obtained evidence that he had followed other employees' cars on previous days.
During the investigation, officials discovered identity cards that had been falsified - including a US passport, California ID card, and a Social Security card with the fake name "Hugo Landry Johns".
A raid on his home in October in East Palo Alto turned up two Russian passports, and a handwritten notebook that contained numerous home addresses of employees "family members' names, educational and employment histories, and assessments of their strengths and weaknesses", prosecutors say.
He faces two charges related his alleged work as a foreign agent, one charge of interstate stalking, and one count of fraud related to his identity documents. He faces over 15 years in prison if found guilty.
- Ukraine's long-range drones using Western tech to hit Russia 
  - Published29 August 2024
He has been held in jail since 2 November. It is unclear whether he has hired a lawyer who can speak on his behalf.
Palantir, which was co-founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, has interests in US defence and security, and has contracts with the Israeli military.
The arrest comes as espionage allegations roil the US tech industry, amid the news that Nvidia ex-CEO Jensen Huang had a romantic affair with a woman suspected of spying for China.
Last month, a former OpenAI employee was charged with planting a listening device in a company office. The man was later accused of having "considerable support" from the Saudi government.

noticias.titulo: Why has Waymo pulled all its driverless cars from US freeways?
noticias.resumen: The vehicles currently operate in 15 US cities, though freeway rides are only offered in a handful, including San Francisco and Los Angeles.
noticias.texto:
Why has Waymo pulled all its driverless cars from US freeways?
Waymo has temporarily suspended driverless rides on US freeways after California banned the service over safety concerns.
California's Department of Motor Vehicles said a series of traffic incidents, including robotaxis entering active construction zones, posed an imminent risk to public safety. Waymo has now restricted freeway operations in all other US markets while it reviews the performance of its vehicles.
Waymo currently operates in 15 US cities, though only offered driverless freeway rides in a handful of cities, including San Francisco and Los Angeles.

noticias.titulo: Catherine visits Mumbai maternity hospital on the last day of royal trip
noticias.resumen: The Prince and Princess of Wales ended their three-day trip to India on Wednesday, the couple's first international tour since 2022.
noticias.texto:
Catherine visits Mumbai maternity hospital on the last day of royal trip
The Prince and Princess of Wales ended their three-day trip to India on Wednesday, the couple's first international tour since 2022.
Catherine visited a maternity hospital in Mumbai and was seen comforting a grieving mother who lost a baby after giving birth to premature twin girls.
William met actors Kareena Kapoor, Saif Ali Khan and filmmaker Karan Johar during a visit to a film production company.
The couple also met Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi, with a Kensington Palace spokesperson saying they discussed the "strength and importance of the UKâIndia bilateral relationship".

noticias.titulo: India's religious make-up - what a new Pew study says about Hindus and Muslims
noticias.resumen: India will remain predominantly Hindu, though its Muslim population is projected to grow faster, according to a new survey.
noticias.texto:
India's religious make-up - what a new Pew study says about Hindus and Muslims
- Published
India will remain overwhelmingly Hindu for decades to come, but its religious composition is projected to shift gradually.
A new study by the Pew Research Center, projecting the world's religious populations to 2070, estimates that Hindus will make up 76% of India's population by then, down from 79% in 2020, while the Muslim share will rise from 15% to 20%.
The shift is rooted largely in differences in age and fertility: Indian Muslims are younger than Hindus and, on average, have more children.
The Pew projections place India at the centre of a wider demographic shift across South Asia.
Pakistan is expected to overtake Indonesia as the country with the world's largest Muslim-majority population, with India moving into second place. Bangladesh, too, is projected to see substantial growth in its Muslim population.
The study projects the religious composition of the world over the next 50-year period, drawing on data from 201 countries and territories, covering virtually the entire global population.
It tracks seven religious groups between 2020 and 2070, assuming recent demographic trends continue. Using census and survey data, it establishes each group's size and age profile in 2020, and factors in differences in fertility and religious switching.
The findings place India at the heart of a changing global religious landscape. The country is expected to have the world's second-largest Muslim population by 2070, after Pakistan, with about 334 million Muslims. Pakistan itself will overtake Indonesia as the country with the largest Muslim population, with an estimated 461 million.
Yet the projections offer little support for the more dramatic narratives sometimes attached to India's changing religious composition.
If current demographic trends continue, the Hindu population in the country is expected to grow by 176 million between 2020 and 2070, the report says. It will continue to account for more than three-quarters of the country's population.
Despite a sharp fall in India's overall fertility, Muslim women still have more children, on average, than Hindu women. Pew attributes the shift primarily to demographic momentum.
Indian Muslims had a median age of 24 in 2020, compared with 29 for Hindus.
Between 2025 and 2030, Pew estimates Muslim women in India will have an average of 2.3 children, against 1.8 among Hindu women.
"We expect religious change in India to be driven almost entirely by long-standing demographic differences between Hindus and Muslims: Muslims are younger and have higher fertility rates," Stephanie Kramer of the Pew Research Center told the BBC.
"The fertility gap has narrowed considerably â from more than one child per woman in 1992 to about half a child in recent years and is likely to keep shrinking," she said.
"But Hindu fertility is already below the replacement level, while Muslim fertility is projected to remain above it for another two decades." (A replacement level is one at which new births are sufficient to maintain a stable population.)
The projections are hardly surprising, says KS James, an Indian demographer at Princeton University.
"The fertility gap between Muslims and Hindus is well established and it means Muslim population growth is likely to remain faster for the next few decades. But fertility is declining across all religious communities and the gap is expected to narrow further," he told the BBC.
"Ultimately, they will converge," he says, adding that the projections do not point to anything dramatically different in India's demographic trajectory.
Demographers push back against claims, often amplified by Hindu right-wing groups, that Muslims will eventually outnumber Hindus. There is no evidence of any significant religious conversion driving population change in India, they say, and the projections do not support such "alarmist scenarios".
The wider South Asian picture is equally revealing, according to the report.
Pakistan's Muslim population is projected to more than double to 461 million by 2070, overtaking Indonesia as the world's largest. India will rank second, with 334 million Muslims, while Bangladesh's Muslim population will rise to 218 million. India and Nepal, meanwhile, will remain the world's only Hindu-majority countries.
There appears to be a global story behind these regional shifts.
By 2035, Muslims are projected to overtake Christians as the world's largest religious group, according to the report. By 2070, their numbers are expected to reach 3.64 billion, up from 2.02 billion in 2020.
Christianity, meanwhile, will have just under three billion followers. Muslims will account for 36% of humanity, compared with 26% today.
But the most dramatic transformation may be taking place thousands of miles west of South Asia, in Africa.
Christianity's centre of gravity is moving steadily away from Europe and the Americas towards sub-Saharan Africa.
The report says that if recent trends continue, more than half of the world's Christians are expected to live there by 2070, compared with 31% in 2020. Pew forecasts that the Democratic Republic of Congo will overtake the United States as the country with the largest Christian population.
The steepest decline is expected to occur in Europe. If current trends continue, by 2070 Europe will be home to 11% of the world's Christian population, down from 22% in 2020, the report says.
The US is projected to lose its Christian majority by 2065, although Christians will remain the country's largest religious group in 2070.
One reason for this changing religious landscape is the growing number of people identifying with no religion.
In UK and France, the "religiously unaffiliated" are projected to become the majority by 2070. South Korea is expected to follow suit.
Yet their share of the world's population is forecast to fall from 24% to 17%, largely because of a decline in China's population.
China accounts for about two-thirds of the world's religiously unaffiliated population. Its expected population decline will more than offset growth in secular populations elsewhere, the report says.
By 2070, there are other unexpected shifts.
The US is projected to become the world's fifth-largest Hindu population, with immigration driving much of its growth.
And Australia's unaffiliated population will overtake Christians as the country's largest group.
Buddhism, meanwhile, faces a demographic squeeze. Its population is expected to fall by more than half in China, Japan and South Korea, reflecting the ageing and shrinking populations of East Asia. Laos and Mongolia are projected to lose their Buddhist majorities.
There are, of course, caveats. These are demographic projections, not predictions of everything that might happen. Pew assumes that recently observed patterns of fertility, migration and religious switching - or conversions - will continue.
"There are many events that could affect religious group populations (including wars, natural disasters, epidemics and changes in economic or social circumstances) that are not analysed here," the report admits.
India's baseline also required projecting the 2020 religious composition from the 2011 census, because the subsequent census had been delayed
Still, the broad direction is unmistakable.
South Asia will remain indispensable to the world's religious story, not just because of India's enormous Hindu population but because of the growing weight of its Muslim populations. Africa will increasingly shape Christianity's future, while Europe and parts of East Asia become more secular.
Clearly, by 2070, the world's religious landscape may look markedly different, shaped less by conversion than by the uneven arithmetic of births, deaths and migration.

noticias.titulo: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?
noticias.resumen: Anthropic's hotly anticipated IPO is expected to put it in the top 10 most valuable US companies, but the future is uncertain.
noticias.texto:
It was during November 2020 that somewhere in San Francisco, a woman called Daniela Amodei phoned a friend, asking for advice.
Daniela oversaw safety and policy at OpenAI, one of the most talked-about AI companies in the world.
But Daniela and her brother Dario - who worked there too - had misgivings over safety levels at OpenAI and thought it could be time to walk away.
So she did what many do when we can't make a decision about something, she phoned a friend. The friend's reply was direct and to the point: "You don't need to be on the phone with me. You already know the answer."
The Amodei siblings and a handful of other colleagues quit. Together, they set up a rival â Anthropic.
Six years on and Anthropic, the maker of leading AI model Claude, has predicted revenues of $52bn in 2026 and $135bn in 2027, according to analyst estimates.
It is about to sell shares to the public for the first time in what's known as an Initial Public Offering or IPO, aiming for a valuation of an estimated $1.4tn (Â£1tn), which would propel it straight into the top 10 of the most valuable US companies.
The sale comes at a crucial time when many are wondering whether, amid increasing concern about the potential of AI, the industry's bubble is showing signs of bursting.
Where once investors were "all in" on a technological revolution to rival the railroads, the car, electricity and the internet, some are now hedging their bets, amid arguments that AI prices will be driven down as the technology becomes more common and concerns that a hefty wedge of the AI investment is tech giants investing in each other.
Shares in companies that supply the raw computing power behind AI, like Coreweave and Nebius, have seen their value cut in half while even the mighty Nvidia has lost its crown as the world's most valuable company with its shares down 30% - a staggering $2tn fall in value.
So could the Anthropic IPO reinflate the bubble or will it be remembered as the last gasp of a boom that is heading for a bust?
A benchmark valuation
At an event last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told JPMorgan Chase's CEO Jamie Dimon that his guiding principle was to "never let your company be worth a single dollar more than it's worth".
The company is selling roughly $65bn worth of shares to the general public and a further $26bn on to other big tech companies. It is comfortably the single biggest money raising event in US corporate history.
It's an old adage that during a gold rush you should buy companies that sell the picks and shovels as opposed to those staking everything on striking gold. In AI's case that's the chip makers, the data centre builders, the energy providers. But Anthropic is arguably the gold itself and this IPO will see what value people put on it, according to Fiona Cincotta.
"I think the reason that this IPO is so important is basically it's the first ability for the public investors to access a pure play AI trade," she says, adding that previous offerings have been about "other parts of the ecosystem, which are, the semiconductors, the chips, the, data centres. But this is the first time that we were actually able to access the AI provider."
What a company is worth depends almost entirely on predicted future earnings.
It's that calculation that many think presents the sharpest needle to the AI bubble.
Will current and future users of AI be prepared to pay enough to justify the trillions being spent on the chips, data centres, energy and employees, some of whom can command annual salaries of over $100m?
"AI is certainly in a financial bubble. While LLMs [large language models] offer genuine utility and are undoubtedly here to stay, the economics don't add up," said Gary Marcus, Professor Emeritus at New York University and author of Taming Silicon Valley, speaking earlier this year.
"[The] more companies build AI models, the [more the] technology becomes commoditised, eliminating meaningful competitive advantages and driving down prices."
So far, the growth rates in Anthropic revenue are extraordinary.
But these explosive growth rates hide a potential problem. Around a quarter of that revenue came from just a handful of companies, among them Google and Amazon.
It's also concentrated in the US which accounts for two-thirds of its revenue.
There is also the staggering network of circular financing found in the AI world. For example, Anthropic has agreements to buy or lease hundreds of billions of dollars worth of chips and computing power from a handful of companies including Broadcom, Google, Amazon. Many of those firms are also investors in Anthropic and major customers of its products.
Public doubts
It's not just some Wall Street investors questioning whether the AI boom is all it's cracked up to be. Out on Main Street, ordinary Americans have concerns too.
With the US driving so much of global AI growth, a growing public backlash against a technology that threatens to replace millions of jobs and hoover up vast amounts of energy and water became a factor in the recent midterm elections in the US.
Many areas in the US have passed moratoriums on data centre development and many candidates deemed too close to big tech found that association a political liability rather than an asset. Many Democrat candidates publicly opposed data centre development and won.
Added to that, the Pied Piper of AI, chip maker Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang, resigned last week after admitting to having been "unfaithful" to his wife after reports he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang.
Huang's spectacular fall from grace and Nvidia's 30% fall in value from its peak have left AI investors looking for a new champion for the AI boom that has underpinned the US stock market and arguably much of its entire economy for the last two years.
If Anthropic â and its CEO are to be AI's new Pied Piper, he will be playing a different tune to the relentlessly upbeat, leather jacket-clad talisman Huang.
While Huang wanted AI development to continue full throttle, Anthropic was built on misgivings over the levels of safety and responsibility the OpenAI leavers felt were being exercised over the development of society-changing technology.
Amodei has warned that AI capabilities could enable biological weapon development, mass surveillance, authoritarianism and the replacement of millions of white-collar, tax-paying workers.
He has called for a slowdown in its development as its powers are growing at such an exponential rate that it could very soon elude any human oversight.
That said, his paternalistic overtures have been sceptically received by those who point out that the pace of Anthropic's development of new more powerful models has shown no sign of the slowdown he's advocating for the rest of the industry.
Hype and FOMO
But for all the concerns, just as with Elon Musk's SpaceX before it â the hype and the FOMO (fear of missing out) on an undoubtedly profound moment in technological and perhaps human development â means that buying interest is high.
It's reported that orders to buy shares exceed the number on offer by over six times.
With demand outstripping supply by such a margin, a first-day jump is likely given the oversubscription, but it doesn't tell you much about long-run return.
Using SpaceX as an example again, shares initially rose nearly 70% from its IPO sale price of $135 to $225. Shares in SpaceX are currently back to $145.
The Anthropic IPO could be wildly successful and blow a bit of fresh new air into what some maintain still looks a lot like a bubble.
Eileen Burbidge, founder of tech investors Passion Capital, is one of those who reject the notion that AI is a bubble about to burst.
"Maybe the growth of the bubble has slowed down a little bit, but actually I wouldn't be willing to say that it's about to burst yet," says Burbidge. "I think this IPO could actually mean everyone could be off to the races again."
Fiona Cincotta believes Anthropic's IPO is about far more than just Anthropic. "I think what's going to be really interesting here is I think it can actually be used as a valuation benchmark for the entire AI ecosystem," she says.
"That's why I don't think this is just going to affect the share price of Anthropic. I think this is going to have much wider implications across the whole AI trade."
Two things can be true at the same time. The Anthropic IPO could be wildly successful - FOMO is a powerful emotion in financial markets. But its probable success won't soothe the unease in some quarters that not every company, every investor and every citizen will think of AI as the answer to humanity's problems.

noticias.titulo: ICJ to rule on Rohingya genocide case against Myanmar
noticias.resumen: The Gambia accuses Myanmar of genocide following a 2017 military crackdown that displaced at least 730,000 Rohingya.
noticias.texto:
ICJ to rule on Rohingya genocide case against Myanmar
The Gambia accused Myanmar of genocide following a 2017 military crackdown displacing over 730,000 Rohingya.
The International Court of Justice (ICJ), the United Nations’ highest court, is set to rule in a landmark case accusing Myanmar of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority.
The reading of the judgment will begin at 10am (09:00 GMT) on Thursday at the Peace Palace in The Hague and is expected to last up to 90 minutes.
It could be the first time the court rules that a state has committed genocide.
The ruling is final and cannot be appealed, but the court has very limited means of enforcing it. If Myanmar ignores it, The Gambia could ask the UN Security Council to act.
What is the case?
The Gambia, a Muslim-majority West African country, brought the case in November 2019 with the backing of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation.
It argues that Myanmar bears state responsibility for genocide resulting from a 2017 military offensive that drove at least 730,000 Rohingya, who are mostly Muslim, from Buddhist-majority Myanmar into Bangladesh.
Survivors have recounted killings, mass rape and the burning of villages. A UN fact-finding mission concluded that the campaign included “genocidal acts”.
Myanmar denies genocide and says its forces responded legitimately to attacks by armed groups. It argues there is no direct evidence of an intent to destroy the Rohingya.
Why is it significant?
Under the 1948 Genocide Convention, genocide requires proof of the specific intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.
The ICJ has never held a state responsible for committing genocide. In 2007, it found that Serbia had failed to prevent the 1995 Srebrenica massacre in Bosnia, in which more than 8,000 Muslim men and boys were killed, but ruled that Serbia had not itself committed genocide.
The judgment could also set precedents for other cases, including South Africa’s case accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza.
The ICJ settles disputes between states, so it can find Myanmar responsible but cannot try individuals, which is the duty of the International Criminal Court.
The Gambia has asked the ICJ to order Myanmar to prosecute those responsible, make reparations and ensure the Rohingya can return safely. Myanmar disputes The Gambia’s right to seek reparations on their behalf.
About 1.2 million Rohingya live in the Cox’s Bazar refugee settlement in Bangladesh, where many will follow the judgment, the Reuters news agency reported. Roughly 550,000 remain in Myanmar, with restrictions on their movement, healthcare and livelihoods.

noticias.titulo: Why a trio of experts alleges Jeffrey Epstein did not die by suicide
noticias.resumen: A new report alleges that injuries on Epstein's body were overlooked by medical examiners during his 2019 autopsy.
noticias.texto:
Why a trio of experts alleges Jeffrey Epstein did not die by suicide
A new report alleges that injuries on Epstein’s body were overlooked by medical examiners during his 2019 autopsy.
A trio of experts has released a report casting doubt on whether convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein died by suicide in his jail cell in 2019, as a medical examiner in the United States previously ruled.
In documents obtained by Al Jazeera and other media outlets, Michael Freeman, Anders Eriksson and Itiel Dror – a forensic scientist, a forensic pathologist and a cognitive scientist – said the injuries on Epstein’s body were “most consistent with homicidal strangulation”, not suicide.
“The pattern, distribution, and multitude of injuries are not explained by a suicidal hanging,” their report reads.
Instead, they suggest Epstein was first assaulted and then strangled, providing an alternative narrative to the medical examiner’s 2019 report.
The cause of Epstein’s death has long been a source of controversy and conspiracy theories.
A wealthy businessman, Epstein cultivated a range of high-profile relationships with leaders in politics, industry, academia and the arts. His network of contacts included US presidents Bill Clinton and Donald Trump.
Those connections have raised questions about whether there was a cover-up of Epstein’s crimes – or whether some of his associates knowingly turned a blind eye.
In 2008, Epstein pleaded guilty to the solicitation of a minor for sex as part of a plea deal that saw him serve 13 months behind bars. Later, in 2019, he was arrested on federal charges of sex trafficking, with prosecutors accusing him of having “sexually exploited and abused dozens of underage girls”.
He died in a New York City jail while awaiting trial.
A controversy over cause of death
Medical examiner Kristin Roman performed the autopsy on Epstein’s body. She and New York City’s Chief Medical Examiner Barbara Sampson ultimately ruled that the evidence pointed to a suicide by hanging.
Other experts have sided with their ruling, pointing out that, while the circumstances of Epstein’s death were unusual, they are not necessarily inconsistent with suicide.
But Epstein’s brother, Mark, has long doubted the medical examiner’s findings. He gave Freeman, an Oregon-based forensic scientist, access to the death records.
Freeman has consulted in trials where families have questioned the narratives put forward by law enforcement about how someone died, including in high-profile cases like the murder of George Floyd.
Eriksson, meanwhile, is a Sweden-based forensic pathologist who has researched issues like shaken baby syndrome, a controversial diagnosis used to prosecute some adults for abuse of young children.
He and Freeman worked alongside Dror, a cognitive scientist who studies biases in forensic science.
At the time of his death, Epstein was a well-known figure, and Dror said the investigators handling his case would have been subject to significant political pressure.
“It’s so obvious this played a critical role in the examination of the body,” Dror told Al Jazeera.
“There was at stake a lot of emotion, a lot of people involved, a lot of politics involved, so many factors. You can list them for an hour, and all of those interfered and biased and influenced what should be a scientific decision.”
Dror explained that he and his colleagues pored over photos and records related to Epstein’s death and concluded that the medical examiner had wrongly ruled it a suicide.
Points of concern raised
In their report, the trio noted a number of issues with the initial investigation.
The prison personnel who found Epstein’s body did not take any photos before moving it, for instance. Investigators also failed to identify the ligature, the object that was actually around Epstein’s neck, they said.
They allege that some avenues of investigation went unexplored. The prison guard who first came across Epstein’s body initially refused to be interviewed, according to the report, and the medical examiner who determined the case was a suicide was not allowed to visit the prison.
The report also disagrees with the medical examiner’s assessment of Epstein’s injuries.
Marks left by the ligature on Epstein’s neck, the researchers said, were not slanted in the way that would be expected if his body had been hanging from the bedpost in his cell.
They observed bruising on Epstein’s back, shoulder and neck that they said was not acknowledged in the medical examiner’s original statements.
Those injuries, their report said, are “most consistent with homicidal strangulation from behind, most likely using a narrow knotted fabric ligature”.
Freeman, Eriksson and Dror believe either that the prison guard who found Epstein was lying about finding his body hanging in the cell, or that the body was deliberately put into that position to make it seem like a suicide had taken place.
