noticias.titulo: German FA backs France’s Diallo for FIFA presidency
noticias.resumen: Incumbent Gianni Infantino has resisted repeated calls to resign, citing overwhelming global support.
noticias.texto:
German FA backs France’s Diallo for FIFA presidency
Incumbent Gianni Infantino has ignored repeated calls to resign, citing overwhelming global support.
The German Football Association (DFB) has said it fully backs French football chief Philippe Diallo’s bid to take over as FIFA president, cementing his support in Europe.
DFB President Bernd Neuendorf announced the endorsement on Wednesday, two days after Diallo, president of the French Football Federation (FFF), accepted UEFA’s support to run against incumbent Gianni Infantino in March. European football’s governing body is eager for change at the top of FIFA.
“Philippe Diallo stands for a responsible approach to football and is determined to tackle the challenges facing the game in the years ahead,” Neuendorf said.
“He has a wealth of experience in international football and is widely respected throughout the European game. His approach to the role and the values he stands for are markedly different from those of the current FIFA president.”
The Dutch football association has also backed Diallo, with many European governing bodies expected to follow suit.
Diallo said on Tuesday that he has the support of countries beyond Europe.
“To beat him [Infantino] you need 106 votes, which is a majority,” he said.
“It is now up to me and my team to go and convince those on other continents, but already since yesterday [Monday] I have received spontaneous signs of strong support which will be revealed in the coming days.”
Opposition to Infantino
Infantino, who has led world football’s governing body since 2016 and is seeking a fourth term, has faced widespread opposition since his July attempt to sell stakes in future World Cups to private investors.
Infantino quickly abandoned the proposal in the face of the uproar, but UEFA has since gone to a court in Florida in an attempt to gather evidence for a potential complaint of “criminal mismanagement” against the FIFA president in Switzerland.
Diallo announced in September that the FFF was withdrawing its backing for Infantino in the election, following similar announcements from other European associations. At the time, he said that “the trust placed in the FIFA president has been betrayed”.
Despite repeated calls for his resignation, Infantino maintains he has overwhelming support from member associations worldwide.
“We want football to change for the better. We want a FIFA that serves the game and acts in the interests of all its member associations,” Neuendorf said.
In addition to Diallo, who has headed the FFF since January 2023, Infantino faces challenges from top Japanese football official Kozo Tashima and Ramon Vega, an ex-Switzerland player.

noticias.titulo: Kenya’s milk shortage deepens as drought hits farmers and pushes up prices
noticias.resumen: Farmers are receiving higher payments but are producing far less milk and also face rising prices for hay.
noticias.texto:
Kenya’s milk shortage deepens as drought hits farmers and pushes up prices
Farmers are receiving higher payments but are producing far less milk and also face rising prices for hay.
Nairobi, Kenya – Milk is becoming harder to find in parts of Kenya as prolonged dry conditions take a toll on dairy farmers, disrupting supplies to major towns and pushing up prices.
In Nairobi, some popular brands have become increasingly difficult to find in shops. A 500ml (1-pint) packet of Tuzo, Dairy Best or Mt Kenya milk sells for 79 to 89 Kenyan shillings ($0.61 to $0.68), but supplies have been limited. New brands have appeared on supermarket shelves at about 65 shillings ($0.50) while some neighbourhood shops visited by Al Jazeera were charging as much as 100 shillings ($0.77) for the same quantity.
The shortage is being felt across the dairy supply chain, from farmers struggling to feed their animals to businesses that depend on a steady supply of fresh milk.
Farmers struggle as pastures dry up
In Kajiado County, southwest of Nairobi, dairy farmers said a prolonged dry spell has sharply reduced milk production over the past three months.
Jennifer Leshinka, a farmer in Bisil, told Al Jazeera that her daily milk production had fallen from 120 litres (32 gallons) to 50 litres (13 gallons). With natural pasture dwindling, she has had to buy hay to feed her animals. Some of her dairy animals have also been moved to neighbouring counties in search of grazing land.
“I supplement the little natural grass with several bales of hay to feed my animals, which has become expensive. A bale of hay is currently retailing between 100 and 150 shillings [$0.77 to $1.15], yet it cannot sustain a mature animal for a day,” Leshinka said.
The pressure is not limited to Kajiado. Diminishing pasture and water supplies are affecting pastoralists in arid and semiarid areas as well as dairy farmers in the highlands, another important milk-producing region.
Jackson Sinkeet, a farmer who supplies raw milk to hotels across the Nairobi metropolitan area, said falling yields have made it difficult to meet orders, even from customers willing to pay higher prices.
He warned that the situation could worsen if dry conditions persist.
Cooperatives and businesses feel the shortage
The decline in production is also affecting dairy cooperatives, which collect milk from farmers and supply major processors.
Jeremiah Ole Ncharo, Kajiado County’s executive committee member in charge of cooperatives, told Al Jazeera that at least five major women-led dairy cooperatives have reported a 50 percent drop in milk deliveries from their members during the dry period.
He said the reduced volumes were affecting supplies to large milk processors, adding to pressure on the formal market.
In Nairobi, hotelier Joram Kamau said businesses were spending hours queuing at major processors’ depots to obtain rationed milk.
The shortage has also raised concerns about the products available in the market. Kamau said he was worried about the growing presence of powdered milk products whose quality and authenticity he questioned. He said he would rather wait for genuine milk, even if it cost more, than risk buying questionable products and losing customers.
Government outlines response as milk supplies fall
Agriculture Cabinet Secretary Mutahi Kagwe told Al Jazeera that the current shortage was largely linked to prolonged dry conditions, which have reduced the availability of pasture, fodder and water, affecting animal productivity and the amount of milk delivered to processors.
He said Kenya’s dairy industry has continued to grow with national milk production rising from 4.64 billion kilogrammes (10.23 billion pounds) in 2021 to 5.52 billion kilogrammes (12.17 billion pounds) in 2025. Formal milk deliveries also increased from about 802 million litres (212 million gallons) to 1.01 billion litres (267 million gallons) over the same period.
However, more recent figures point to a decline in milk reaching formal processors. Kagwe said monthly deliveries averaged about 83.45 million litres (22 million gallons) in 2025, compared with 74.09 million litres (19.57 million gallons) in September.
He said the decline has affected volumes available for processing, particularly UHT milk, which has a longer shelf life and helps maintain supplies.
However, government market surveillance for the week ending October 30 indicated a slight improvement in UHT milk availability across most parts of the country. Other dairy products, including fermented milk, butter and cheese, were generally available at normal stock levels.
Kagwe said the government was monitoring production, processor stocks, producer prices and retail prices. It was also facilitating regional transfers of milk and dairy products, particularly within the East African Community, while encouraging processors to collect more milk from farmers and cooperatives.
He added that farmers were receiving better prices amid tighter supplies. The average gross producer price rose to about 53.88 shillings ($0.41) per litre (1 quart) in July, compared with an average of 49.58 shillings ($0.38) in 2025.
Buffalo proposal offers no immediate relief
To address longer-term challenges in the dairy sector, the government is looking at ways to increase production and improve farmers’ resilience.
Kagwe said planned measures included expanding fodder production and conservation, continuing a subsidised artificial insemination programme to improve dairy genetics and distributing milk coolers to organised farmer groups. The restructuring of the state-owned dairy processor New KCC is also expected to improve services to producers and consumers.
The government is also exploring President William Ruto’s proposal to introduce Indian water buffaloes to Kenya as an additional source of milk.
Kagwe told Al Jazeera that the initiative was still at an early stage. Kenya would first need to establish veterinary and import requirements, identify suitable breeds and sources, and bring in a limited number of animals to assess their adaptability and productivity under local conditions.
India, the world’s largest milk producer, relies on buffaloes for about 43 percent of its milk production. Buffalo milk has a relatively high fat and solids content, making it suitable for products such as cheese and butter.
But Kagwe said the proposal should be seen as a medium- to long-term opportunity rather than a response to the current shortage.
For farmers such as Leshinka and Sinkeet, the immediate challenge remains the rising cost of keeping their animals fed and productive. In Nairobi, businesses are still struggling to secure enough milk to meet customer demand.
“The animals’ milk yield has dropped significantly. I am unable to supply my customers, who are willing to pay higher prices, because the milk is simply not available,” Sinkeet told Al Jazeera.

noticias.titulo: Somalia’s constitutional overhaul tests its fragile federal bargain
noticias.resumen: Mohamud’s reforms promise stronger government, but regional resistance and violence threaten the fragile deal of 2012.
noticias.texto:
Somalia’s constitutional overhaul tests its fragile federal bargain
President Mohamud’s reforms promise stronger government, but regional resistance and violence threaten the fragile deal of 2012.
Mogadishu, Somalia – A day before Somalia’s Supreme Court was due to rule on whether President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud had lawfully extended his term by a year, he abruptly dismissed the chief justice presiding over the case.
On November 4, the presidency removed Chief Justice Bashe Yusuf Ahmed, citing complaints about the administration of justice. Five judges proceeded with the case the following day, ruling that constitutional amendments extending presidential and parliamentary terms from four to five years could not apply retrospectively to those already in office. Their mandates, the judges said, had expired.
The government rejected the ruling and immediately swore in a replacement chief justice, setting up a direct confrontation between the president and the country’s highest court over the end of his mandate and the timing of elections.
The standoff marks the latest escalation in a two-year political contest over Mohamud’s proposed constitutional changes.
Intended to address long-standing structural problems that have hindered Somalia’s reconstruction, the changes have instead deepened divisions over the country’s political future, the nature of its federal system and the distribution of power.
Mohamud and his allies believe stronger national institutions, clearer rules and direct elections will help advance Somalia’s decades-long state-building project.
The deadlock has increasingly spilled beyond parliament and political negotiations, with tensions playing out on the ground.
Two federal states have suspended cooperation with Mogadishu, while disputes elsewhere have turned violent. In June, clashes between government forces and militias guarding a former president and prime minister brought part of the capital to a standstill for two days.
A federal bargain left unfinished
Somalia’s effort to rebuild a functioning national government is one of the world’s longest-running state-building efforts, hampered by a decades-long civil war.
After the central government collapsed in 1991, regional administrations emerged around clan alliances, building their own institutions, security forces and revenue streams.
Somaliland was the first to emerge from the ashes of Somalia’s civil war, declaring independence in 1991. Puntland followed in 1998, establishing an autonomous administration. Other regional administrations emerged in subsequent years, eventually forming part of the country’s evolving federal system.
The provisional constitution adopted in 2012 established a federal framework for sharing power between Mogadishu and the regions. However, some of the most contentious questions over the division of powers and control of resources were deferred as national institutions took shape.
Those unresolved questions made governance dependent on constant negotiation. Elections depended on agreements among regional leaders and clan elders, while disputes over power and revenue repeatedly delayed national decisions in the absence of consensus.
“Control of ports and trade routes, and relationships with foreign governments, gave some considerable independence from Mogadishu,” Jethro Norman, a Somalia expert at the Danish Institute for International Studies, told Al Jazeera.
Norman said Mohamud’s overhaul seeks to give Mogadishu greater legal authority over areas that regional administrations have long controlled, although enforcing that authority is another matter.
“What you’re seeing is the federal system crystallising into two camps,” he told Al Jazeera. “You have Villa Somalia presenting the constitution as completing the state: one person, one vote, multi-party politics, democracy, central federal control over foreign relations and national security, and so on.”
Puntland and Jubaland, by contrast, see the changes as an imposition that undermines the original federal bargain.
“Their view is that the 2012 constitution was a bargain between the centre and the regions, and it can’t just be re-written through a parliamentary majority in Mogadishu when the regions have rejected it,” Norman said.
Some federal states retain close commercial and security ties with the United Arab Emirates (UAE), which Mohamud, who has frosty ties with Abu Dhabi, has accused of supporting regional leaders in their disputes with Mogadishu.
In January, Mohamud’s government announced the cancellation of the UAE’s port and security agreements across Somalia. The regional states, however, rejected the decision.
The dispute has added to tensions over the future of the federation. Puntland President Said Abdullahi Deni, whose administration is among Somalia’s most autonomous, has even suggested that the country may need to reconsider how it holds together.
“If a solution is not found for the current debate, Somalis must deliberate and decide on another alternative way to live together,” he warned.
The stakes have also grown with international recognition of Somaliland. Israel became the first United Nations member state to recognise the breakaway northern region at the end of 2025.
Somali academic Afyare Elmi told Al Jazeera that the government was weakening the fragile consensus underpinning the 2012 settlement by pushing through constitutional changes it could not enforce in states that opposed them.
“This is one of the most dangerous times the Somali political system has faced,” he said. “Somalis are no longer moving in the same direction on the future of the state.”
Completing the constitution
Mohamud himself helped shape the federal system he is now seeking to overhaul.
During his first presidency, from 2012 to 2017, his government participated in negotiations to establish or consolidate several federal member states. After returning to office in 2022, he oversaw the creation of another state and made completing the constitution and introducing direct elections key priorities.
Yet the boundaries of some federal states remain disputed, reflecting what Elmi, the Somali academic, described as the haphazard way in which the federal system was assembled.
Parliament passed the first constitutional amendments in 2024 and approved the remaining changes in March 2026, bringing a 14-year review process to a close. The overhaul seeks to resolve questions about the division of powers that Somalia’s leaders left unsettled in 2012.
The changes give Mogadishu greater authority over revenue collection and sharing, elections and the conditions under which the federal government can intervene in member states.
They also provide for citizens to elect members of the federal lower house directly through a national electoral commission, although parliament will continue to choose the president.
Though Mohamud helped establish several federal member states during his first presidency, Elmi questioned whether he had ever intended for them to exercise significant autonomy from Mogadishu.
“Hassan Sheikh always wanted a Mogadishu-centred federal state, with no real federal substance,” he said.
Ali Mohamed Omar, Somalia’s state minister for foreign affairs, told Al Jazeera that the previous system, under which clan elders and delegates selected members of parliament, had left successive governments without the public legitimacy they needed.
Retaining parliament’s power to elect the president, rather than introducing a direct presidential vote, was a compromise intended to secure the support of some opposition groups, Omar said.
Mohamed Ibrahim Moalimuu, a federal lawmaker who supports the overhaul, described the president’s decision to press ahead as “daring”. Successive governments had tried and failed to complete the constitution, he said, while most Somalis had yet to gain the right to elect their national representatives directly.
“Somalia cannot just remain stuck just because the changes made aren’t considered perfect for everyone,” he told Al Jazeera.
For regional presidents and clan elders, however, the changes threaten to diminish their influence over the selection of members of parliament and weaken the political leverage they have built up in negotiations with Mogadishu.
Puntland rejected the first amendments in 2024 and withdrew its cooperation with the federal government. Jubaland followed after a dispute over electoral legislation.
Both have their own security forces and revenue sources, and their leaders argue that agreements reached without their participation cannot be imposed on them.
Elections and political power
The consequences have been most pronounced in South West state, where a dispute over President Abdiaziz Hassan Laftagareen’s re-election in March has escalated into a struggle for control of Baidoa, the regional capital.
Mogadishu rejected the vote and federal troops ousted him. Since then, forces loyal to Laftagareen have seized several strategic towns around the city and clashed with government troops.
Following Laftagareen’s removal, South West held Somalia’s first direct election for a federal state assembly in May, a milestone for Mohamud’s reforms. The newly elected lawmakers chose Mohamud ally Sheikh Adan Mohamed Nur Madobe as regional president the following month.
Laftagareen, now in exile in Nairobi alongside senior members of his former administration, told Al Jazeera he intended to return to Baidoa and remove Madobe’s government from power.
He said he had repeatedly warned Mohamud against changing the constitution without first building broader consensus among the country’s political elite.
“Separating powers between the centre and the regional governments saved and kept Somalia together, and making these changes is driving the country apart,” he said.
Not all federal states oppose Mohamud’s reforms. His allies now lead four of Somalia’s six states, where recent elections have also strengthened his Justice and Solidarity Party.
But the outcome in Hirshabelle, one of those states, has prompted further resistance in its Hiiraan region, where political leaders and elders say long-standing grievances over political representation have yet to be addressed. Armed fighters have occupied parts of the regional administration’s offices in Beledweyne.
Moalimuu acknowledged that the recent elections “weren’t totally free and fair”, but argued that giving citizens the opportunity to vote was an important first step.
The electoral commission has scheduled parliamentary elections for April 15, 2027, followed by parliament’s election of the president on May 15. The timetable is based on the new five-year terms, even though the Supreme Court ruled that the extension could not apply to officials already in office.
Mohamed Mahmoud Dirie, a spokesperson for the Somali Future Council, a coalition of politicians including former presidents and prime ministers, said the group had rejected Mohamud’s invitation to talks in November.
“Our request for a guarantor from the international community for whatever is agreed was rejected, which will make it difficult to ensure that the government holds to its side of the bargain,” Dirie said.
The political divisions are deepening as international support for Somalia’s reconstruction comes under growing pressure. The UN political mission, which supported Somalia’s constitutional negotiations, elections and reconciliation efforts, closed in October at the government’s request.
The African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), which is supporting Somali forces in their fight against al-Shabab, also faces funding shortages and uncertainty over continued UN logistical support for its operations.
Uganda has begun withdrawing its bilateral troops and plans to withdraw its AUSSOM contingent by the end of 2027, while humanitarian aid is also shrinking.
“Somalia is going through multiple difficult transitions,” Mahad Wasuge, executive director of the Mogadishu-based think tank Somali Public Agenda, told Al Jazeera.
Wasuge said these changes could leave Somalia increasingly exposed at a time when “the trust between elites is low”.

noticias.titulo: Anthropic raises $81.3bn in biggest IPO of all time
noticias.resumen: AI giant prices shares at $83 in blockbuster market debut.
noticias.texto:
Anthropic raises $81.3bn in biggest IPO of all time
AI giant prices shares at $83 in blockbuster market debut.
Anthropic has raised $81.3bn in the largest initial public offering (IPO) in history, leapfrogging SpaceX’s initial $75bn market debut in June.
The AI giant said in a statement late on Wednesday that the company and its seven co-founders had sold 980 million shares at $83 each.
The bigger-than-expected IPO comes after investor demand for the stock far outstripped forecasts.
The company had said in corporate filings last week that it intended to offer 825 million shares at between $70 and $78 apiece.
The blockbuster offering puts Anthropic, founded in 2021 by former researchers from rival AI firm OpenAI, on track for a market value of roughly $1.5 trillion, which would make it the world’s 12th-biggest firm at current valuations, just behind Tesla.
Anthropic shares will begin trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange in New York on Thursday under the ticker “ANT”.
The company’s market debut has been closely watched as a test of the eye-watering valuations of tech companies leading the AI rollout.
Tech firms have poured trillions of dollars into AI, expecting it to usher in revolutionary changes in business and society.
AI-related spending is forecast to reach $2.7 trillion in 2026 and $3.6 trillion in 2027, according to technology insights company Gartner. Companies betting on the frontier technology currently make up roughly half of the value of the S&P 500 index.
The spending frenzy has stoked debate over whether Big Tech is funding a future gold mine or a speculative bubble like the one that preceded the 2000 dot-com crash.
Jay R Ritter, an IPO expert at the University of Florida, called Anthropic’s valuation unprecedented for such a young company.
“Investors are excited about its software, which may allow drug companies to find drugs capable of preventing cancer and dementia within ten years,” Ritter told Al Jazeera.
“Thirty years ago, the internet was the next big thing. It has changed our lives. Today, artificial intelligence is the next big thing,” he said.
More to follow…

noticias.titulo: Unvaccinated Pennsylvania resident dies amid historic US measles resurgence
noticias.resumen: Pennsylvania records eighth measles death of 2026, a day after the US formally loses its 26-year elimination status.
noticias.texto:
Unvaccinated Pennsylvania resident dies amid historic US measles resurgence
Pennsylvania records eighth measles death of 2026, a day after the US formally loses its 26-year elimination status.
An unvaccinated resident of Pennsylvania has died after contracting measles, marking the eighth measles-related fatality in the northeastern state this year.
The Pennsylvania Department of Health (DOH) confirmed the death on Wednesday and said it had been reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
While the department did not publicly identify the individual who died, it said they were a resident of Clinton County, in the centre of the state.
The latest death comes shortly after the United States formally lost its measles elimination status, a designation it held for nearly 26 years.
That status indicated that measles was not endemic to the US, meaning no single strain had circulated continuously for 12 months or more.
The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a branch of the World Health Organization, updated the US’s designation on Tuesday after reviewing transmission data from the country.
The US is grappling with its worst measles outbreak in more than three decades. As of November 12, the CDC had counted 5,412 confirmed cases since the start of the year.
Pennsylvania, meanwhile, reported 1,589 cases across 46 of its 67 counties. The state’s health agency pledged to continue its aggressive response to the outbreak.
“Approximately 300 DOH staff are proactively working with residents, community organizations, and health care providers to combat the measles outbreak in the Commonwealth through access to fact-based information and access to the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine,” the department wrote in a news release.
The agency also said state health officials have administered more than 11,500 MMR vaccine doses in 2026, including more than 7,200 shots in pop-up clinics since the outbreak erupted in late April.
Experts say vaccine hesitancy in recent decades has contributed to the rising number of cases.
Measles is highly contagious and can spread quickly, particularly when someone coughs or sneezes. The virus can survive for up to two hours in the air, and an estimated 90 percent of those who are not immune will catch it upon exposure, according to medical authorities.
Critics point to leadership under US President Donald Trump as contributing to the measles outbreaks.
One of Trump’s cabinet officials, Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, has questioned the efficacy and safety of vaccines like the MMR shot.
He also said in an interview with NewsNation that the MMR vaccine “contains a lot of aborted foetus debris and DNA particles”, an unsubstantiated claim.
Still, he encouraged vaccination in a social media post on Tuesday, following PAHO’s decision to revoke the US’s measles elimination status.
“We will stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status. I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles,” he wrote.
The CDC also said it remained committed to stopping measles outbreaks and regaining the country’s elimination status.
“The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does,” CDC Director Erica Schwartz said.
Before taking office in early 2025, Kennedy claimed that no vaccine was “safe and effective” and promoted the discredited theory that vaccines cause autism.

noticias.titulo: EU governments approve trade deal with Indonesia to offset Trump tariffs
noticias.resumen: The deal, initially concluded in 2025, will see both sides remove import duties on more than 90 percent of products.
noticias.texto:
EU governments approve trade deal with Indonesia to offset Trump tariffs
The deal, initially concluded in 2025, will see both sides remove import duties on more than 90 percent of products.
European Union governments have approved the signing of a previously agreed trade deal between the EU and Indonesia aimed at offsetting the impact of United States President Donald Trump’s tariffs.
The Council of the European Union’s decision on Wednesday also allows the deal to be applied provisionally. Both sides will remove import duties on more than 90 percent of products, and Indonesia’s 50 percent duty on EU cars will be eliminated within five years.
The deal will tie one of the world’s top economic blocs more closely to the fourth most populous country.
“These agreements will make it easier for European businesses to trade and invest, remove tariffs on almost all goods traded between the EU and Indonesia, and save businesses an estimated €600 million [$658.3m] annually in customs duties,” said Irish Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade Helen McEntee.
Indonesia has been negotiating a free trade and investment agreement with the EU since 2016. However, relations became strained after the European Commission decided to phase out palm oil from transport fuel by 2030 and imposed anti-subsidy duties on Indonesia’s biodiesel exports.
Both sides want the agreement, initially concluded in September 2025, to be applied as swiftly as possible. Indonesia will graduate from the EU’s generalised scheme of preferences on January 1, 2027, after which its exports will no longer benefit from preferential tariffs, the Council said in a statement.
The EU and Indonesia will now sign the agreements, which will then be submitted to the European Parliament for approval.

noticias.titulo: Migrant boat capsizes off Senegal, leaving at least one dead
noticias.resumen: Incident comes days after another boat capsized in Senegalese waters, and Spain declared a migration emergency.
noticias.texto:
Migrant boat capsizes off Senegal, leaving at least one dead
Incident comes 10 days after another boat capsized in Senegalese waters, killing 43 migrants.
A small boat carrying migrants and refugees has capsized off the coast of Yenne in western Senegal, killing at least one person.
Local officials told the AFP news agency that the pirogue-type flat-bottomed boat struck a rocky area and washed ashore overnight from Tuesday to Wednesday.
A survivor of the shipwreck who was questioned by the gendarmerie said that there were about 100 people on board the boat, including five women, according to a local elected official.
Yenne Mayor Massamba Mbengue and local firefighters said that one body was recovered, while two other local sources put the body count at two.
Oumar Sow, a representative of the village chief, said that the incident “occurred around 2:00am [02:00 GMT]. Cries could be heard coming from the pirogue that were audible even from the beach”.
Smugglers
The boat washed up on the beach in a dilapidated state, according to eyewitnesses.
A gendarmerie commander sorted items that were found on the boat, including water sachets and personal belongings.
Eight identity documents, several mobile phones and a school enrolment document belonging to a high school student from Kabrousse, in Senegal’s south, were also discovered, according to the local official.
The official said Yenne has become a migration embarkation point, with smugglers coming to the village to recruit boat pilots.
The latest incident comes just 10 days after a shipwreck off the coast of the northwestern town of Thieppe killed 43 people, in one of the deadliest migration disasters in Senegal’s history.
Human rights group Action for Human Rights and Friendship (ADHA) in Senegal called on the government to conduct a parliamentary inquiry into the tragedy.
In a statement released at the time, ADHA denounced a “lack of lasting results” to reduce migrant deaths at sea.
Record numbers reach Spain
Spain declared a migration emergency in the Canary Islands on November 10 after the arrival of more than 9,000 people in its Atlantic Ocean territory since the start of November.
Spain’s Maritime Rescue Service said it had rescued 1,488 migrants aboard 14 dinghies, most of whom arrived on El Hierro in the Canary Islands from West Africa on November 14.
That broke the record of 1,461 people rescued six years earlier in November 2020.
Most migrants arriving in El Hierro depart from West Africa, often from Senegal, hoping to reach mainland Europe.
Last month, Spain deported more than a dozen of the 80,000 people who entered its North African enclave of Ceuta from Morocco over 48 hours in late July.
At least 100 people died during the mass crossing into the autonomous city, which covers just 18.5 square kilometres (7.1sq miles) and has a population of about 80,000.

noticias.titulo: NASA’s Voyager 1 hits record one light-day distance, 50 years after launch
noticias.resumen: Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth, marking a historic milestone nearly 50 years after its 1977 launch.
noticias.texto:
NASA’s Voyager 1 hits record one light-day distance, 50 years after launch
Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth, marking a historic milestone nearly 50 years after its 1977 launch.
NASA’s Voyager 1 probe, the most distant human-made object, has reached a distance of one light-day from Earth nearly 50 years after it was launched.
The spacecraft hit the milestone on Wednesday and is now about 26 billion km away, according to NASA.
A light-day is the distance light can travel in 24 hours, which means messages sent from Earth take a day to reach Voyager 1, and another day for teams on the ground to receive a reply.
The feat is “the best illustration of just how vast space is”, said NASA scientist Tiffany Kataria. “So much of what we dream about is travelling to other stellar systems,” she told the AFP news agency. “And it took Voyager 1 nearly 50 years to get to just the edge of our own solar system, let alone to only a light-day.”
Many exoplanetary systems, she noted, are at least several light-years away. NASA expects Voyager 1 to take about 18,000 years to travel a full light-year.
Interstellar space
Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 and its twin Voyager 2 are the only spacecraft to have reached interstellar space, the region beyond the Sun’s heliosphere. Voyager 2 is expected to reach one light-day in 2035.
Some of Voyager 1’s equipment, including its cameras, has been switched off remotely to save power, but the probe continues to study invisible phenomena such as magnetic fields.
The data helps researchers study “the gas, the dust and other material that exists between stars”, Kataria said.
Both craft carry “Golden Records”, 30cm gold-plated copper discs intended to convey the story of our world to extraterrestrials.
Earlier in their journeys, the Voyagers explored the giant planets Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.
Images of Jupiter taken by Voyager 1 first revealed the existence of rings around the planet and helped scientists understand the “really extreme vortices and weather” in its atmosphere, Kataria added.

noticias.titulo: US steps up pressure on Iran-backed Hezbollah with new sanctions
noticias.resumen: The US Treasury has accused Hezbollah of using charitable organisations as 'fronts' for fundraising.
noticias.texto:
US steps up pressure on Iran-backed Hezbollah with new sanctions
The US Treasury has accused Hezbollah of using charitable organisations as ‘fronts’ for fundraising.
US deports Lebanese consul-general in Detroit over Hezbollah praise
The United States has announced new sanctions targeting a group that it says serves as a “front organisation” for the Lebanese group Hezbollah, which Washington considers a “terrorist” entity.
On Wednesday, the US Treasury said it had designated the Wa Ta’awanu Association, named for the Arabic words for “and cooperate”, the first two words of a popular Quranic verse.
It described the organisation as a “Hizballah-affiliated charity that provides cover for Hizballah’s activities under the guise of delivering humanitarian services”.
Three people based in Lebanon were also sanctioned. They include the Wa Ta’awanu Association’s founder, Afif Abdel Rida Chouman, and two businessman brothers, Hassan Khechen and Ibrahim Khechen, accused of funnelling money from Iran to Hezbollah.
Two gold companies the brothers reportedly operate were added to the US sanctions list as well.
The administration of US President Donald Trump framed the added sanctions as part of its overarching effort to dismantle Hezbollah’s financial networks and cut off resources for Iran’s proxies.
“The Iranian regime’s attempts to infringe on Lebanon’s sovereignty through terror proxies like Hizballah will not be tolerated,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement.
Since February 28, the US and its ally Israel have waged war against Iran, on the alleged premise that a military offensive was necessary to prevent Tehran from gaining nuclear weapons.
Iran, however, has long denied such ambitions, claiming its uranium enrichment programme is instead for civilian energy infrastructure.
Hezbollah, one of Iran’s regional allies, has been designated a “foreign terrorist organisation” in the US since 1997.
In Wednesday’s statement, the US Treasury accused civilian charitable organisations and humanitarian assistance efforts of channelling “outside donor funds toward Hezbollah’s terrorist activities”.
While Trump earlier this month claimed the conflict with Iran was “effectively over” from a military standpoint, US forces struck Iran’s Qeshm Island this week.
The US also continues to maintain a naval blockade, as well as an effort — dubbed Task Force Iron Gate — to prevent Iran from receiving supplies by land or the Caspian Sea.
To support that effort, the US aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt recently arrived in the Middle East.
Hours before Wednesday’s designations, the US military published a new advisory saying that it would treat ships receiving cargo at sea from vessels loaded in Iran as an attempt to evade its blockade. It warned it could take action against such vessels.
Last week, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told foreign ministers from the Group of Seven (G7) forum that the US would keep imposing “devastating” economic costs on Iran.
Hezbollah has denounced previous US sanctions, calling them an “attempt to intimidate the free Lebanese people”. It added that such economic penalties would have “absolutely no practical effect” on its “strategic choices”.

noticias.titulo: Iraq sentences six French nationals to life in prison for joining ISIL
noticias.resumen: Trials began in September for 47 French citizens who were transferred from Syria last year.
noticias.texto:
Iraq sentences six French nationals to life in prison for joining ISIL
Trials began in September for 47 French citizens who were transferred from Syria last year.
An Iraqi criminal court has sentenced six French nationals to life in prison for joining the ISIL (ISIS) group, state media reported.
The Karkh Criminal Court delivered the sentencing on Wednesday with representatives from the French embassy in attendance, the Iraqi News Agency (INA) reported, citing Iraq’s judiciary.
“With these six sentences, the total number of those convicted in this case has reached 16, all of whom are French nationals,” the judiciary said in a statement cited by INA.
All but one of the 16 convicted were sentenced to life. The court sentenced one defendant to 15 years in prison last month.
Trials began in September for 47 French citizens who were transferred from Syria last year and charged with belonging to the armed group, which controlled large parts of both countries between 2014 and 2017.
In February, Iraq received more than 5,700 ISIL detainees from over 60 countries after the United States transferred them from Syria, following years of detention in prisons run by Kurdish-led forces.
For years, Iraqi courts handed down hundreds of execution orders and life sentences to people convicted of “terrorism” offences, including foreign fighters. However, some rights groups denounced the trials as rushed and lacking due process.
Among the foreign fighters sentenced on Wednesday was Thomas Barnouin, a 45-year-old Frenchman, who said during his trial that he travelled to Syria convinced he had a religious duty and did not know ISIL would carry out attacks in France, according to AFP.
The ISIL group swept across Syria and Iraq in 2014, committing massacres and forcing women and girls into sexual slavery.
Iraq, backed by US-led forces, proclaimed victory over the group in 2017, and Kurdish-led forces supported by Washington defeated ISIL in neighbouring Syria two years later.
Iraq is nonetheless still reckoning with the group’s legacy, with mass graves being uncovered and testimonies of its brutality still to be investigated.

noticias.titulo: US lawmakers push to raise minimum wage to $25, end tipped pay system
noticias.resumen: Public support for raising the minimum wage grows, with 78 percent of voters saying it was an important election issue.
noticias.texto:
US lawmakers push to raise minimum wage to $25, end tipped pay system
Public support for raising the minimum wage grows, with 78 percent of voters saying it was an important election issue.
In Washington, DC, a group of lawmakers has ramped up calls to increase the United States federal minimum wage and eliminate the subminimum wage, otherwise known as the tipped wage.
The group of 17 lawmakers, which includes current and newly elected House members, is calling for passage of the Living Wage For All Act, which has been languishing since it was introduced in April.
The legislation’s original lead sponsors include Representative Delia Ramirez of Illinois, Representative Jesus “Chuy” Garcia, also of Illinois, and Representative Analilia Mejia of New Jersey.
The bill aims to gradually raise the federal minimum wage to $25 an hour, with different timelines depending on the size of the employer.
Brad Lander, a congressman-elect from Brooklyn, New York, who says he will join the bill as a co-sponsor when the next congressional session begins in January, told Al Jazeera: “Doing it federally is the right way to go. Tying it into broader legislation that raises the minimum wage for all workers is a great approach.”
For larger employers — those with more than 500 employees nationwide or at least $1bn in annual revenue — the increase would be completed by 2031. Smaller employers would have until 2038.
After that, the minimum wage would be maintained at two-thirds of the US median hourly wage, with annual adjustments to preserve that ratio.
The bill would also eliminate the separate subminimum wage for tipped workers, currently $2.13 an hour. Under the existing framework, employers can count workers’ tips towards their minimum-wage requirements.
While several states have raised their own minimum wages, the federal rate remains $7.25 an hour, where it has stood since 2009. Washington, DC, has the highest minimum wage of any US jurisdiction, at $18.40 an hour, followed by Washington state at $17.13. However, 20 states do not have a minimum wage higher than the federal rate. Those states include Texas, Georgia and Iowa.
Laws governing the subminimum wage also vary across states. Seven states require employers to pay tipped workers the full minimum wage before tips, including Alaska, California and Nevada.
Others, including New York, have higher tipped cash wages than the federal rate but allow employers to take a tip credit, meaning they can pay workers less than the standard minimum wage as long as their tips make up the difference.
In New York, minimum wages vary by region. The rate is $17 an hour in New York City and its surrounding suburbs, and $16 an hour in the rest of the state.
For tipped workers outside the food service industry, the minimum cash wage is $14.15 in the New York City metropolitan area and $13.30 elsewhere in the state. For restaurant workers, those rates are $11.35 and $10.70, respectively.
The distinction is a point of contention for Lander.
“All workers deserve a raise. The 45 million working people who make less than $20 an hour deserve a raise, and the tipped subminimum wage is inexcusable at this point,” he said.
A long-term fight
The subminimum wage has long been viewed as a legacy of racial and economic inequalities that disproportionately affected Black Americans. When Congress passed the Fair Labor Standards Act in 1938, establishing the first federal minimum wage, it excluded categories of workers in domestic and agricultural occupations, which disproportionately employed Black Americans.
Congress extended federal minimum-wage protections to restaurant and other service workers in 1966. But rather than requiring employers to pay tipped workers the full minimum wage, lawmakers established a separate tipped minimum wage, initially set at 50 percent of the standard federal rate. Employers could count customers’ tips towards the rest of a worker’s minimum-wage obligation. In 1996, Congress froze the federal tipped cash wage at $2.13 an hour, where it remains today.
The purchasing power of the standard federal minimum wage has also changed drastically. Adjusted for inflation, the $7.25 minimum wage in 2009 would be worth $11.32 today, meaning it has lost 36 percent of its purchasing power.
The federal minimum wage’s purchasing power peaked in 1968, when the rate was $1.60 an hour. Adjusted for inflation, that peak would be worth significantly more than the current minimum wage, representing a loss of roughly 53 percent in purchasing power.
The push to raise wages also has public support. A new poll released on Wednesday by One Fair Wage, an organisation that has long campaigned to eliminate the subminimum wage, found that 78 percent of voters considered raising the minimum wage to $25 an hour an important factor in their vote in the recent US midterm elections, where Republicans were dealt massive losses with the cost of living a key issue for voters.
“Washington has allowed the federal minimum wage to become increasingly disconnected from the economic reality facing American families,” Saru Jayaraman, president of One Fair Wage, said in a statement.
The push for the Living Wage For All Act comes as Democrats prepare to take control of both the House and Senate in the new Congress.
The last major attempt to raise the federal minimum wage came during former President Joe Biden’s first year in office. Democrats sought to increase the rate from $7.25 to $15 an hour through the Raise the Wage Act of 2021, which was included in the original proposal for Biden’s American Rescue Plan.
Ultimately, the effort failed after the Senate rejected a motion to waive budgetary rules that would have allowed the minimum-wage increase to proceed. The March 2021 vote was 42–58, with all Republicans opposed, joined by seven Democrats and independent Senator Angus King of Maine, who caucuses with Democrats.
Although the legislation failed, Biden raised the minimum wage for federal contract workers to $15 an hour in 2022 through an executive order. President Donald Trump revoked that order in 2025.
