noticias.titulo: [Interview] Czech MEP Niedermayer slams Babiš opposition to new EU budget revenue: ‘It’s short-sighted’
noticias.resumen: From missed IT revolutions to costly nuclear bets, EU Parliament's economic policy vice-chair Luděk Niedermayer sketches a stark choice for European capitals: keep blaming Brussels for their woes, clinging to national budgets, or allow the EU to levy its own targeted taxes on negative externalities to better compete with the US and China.
noticias.texto: The EU should introduce its own taxes to discourage the consumption of harmful products such as tobacco and strengthen its ability to compete with the US and China, Czech MEP Luděk Niedermayer said in an interview. A member of the centre-right European People’s Party (EPP), Niedermayer is a former vice-governor of the Czech central bank and vice-chair of the European Parliament’s committee on economic and monetary affairs. The 2024 report of former Italian prime minister Mario Draghi delivered a n unflattering assessment of the EU’s competitiveness . Do you fear that divisions between national capitals in the EU means the union will have to rely on enhanced cooperation more often? Luděk Niedermayer: I would not describe enhanced cooperation as something to fear — in many cases, it is a useful solution when all countries simply do not agree on something that would in fact move the EU forward. As an MEP, I worked on a mechanism to promote equity financing for companies instead of loans. In my view, that mechanism is very good and has clear economic justification. It stalled in the Council, blocked by the unanimity requirement for tax matters. “National leaders declare their support for Draghi’s findings, but do precisely the opposite in negotiations on the European budget.” But if, through enhanced cooperation, a workable concept could be created for a group of countries without undermining the single market, it would clearly add value. The same applies to the so-called 28th legal regime [ EU Inc ]. If someone offered me a choice between a weak compromise and a strong regime for half of the EU’s member states, I would choose the latter. The red line is fragmentation of the single market itself, for instance by protectionist barriers between member states. It cannot be that someone says: ‘I am in the single market, but I do not import apples from Poland,’ or, ‘I am in the single market, but I will not import cars from Czechia and Slovakia.’ That would be the end of the road, but nobody is considering that. So what follows from this? The Draghi report focuses on key European sectors for economic growth. Many member states blame their economic failures on EU regulations, while other countries operating within the same legislative framework achieve excellent results, prosper and reduce their debt. National leaders declare their support for Draghi’s findings, but do precisely the opposite in negotiations on the European budget. [Another former Italian prime minister] Enrico Letta’s report on the single market is equally crucial. It outlines changes that could be implemented more quickly. You are working on the 28th regime with former Slovak prime minister and current Renew MEP Ľudovít Ódor with the aim to enable companies to grow without having to hire dozens of tax advisers in each EU country. Given that taxation falls within national competence, is it realistic to establish a workable model? I consider the EU Commission’s initial proposal to simplify the establishment of companies across borders good. Digitalisation, simplification and acceleration are a good direction to take as a starting point. Read more EU unveils ’28th regime’, creating bloc-wide business code I do not think it is essential for the 28th regime to be used by tens of thousands of companies across the EU; it would be most effective for start-ups and expanding companies, for which the costs of extending across Europe are greatest. Limiting this regime to a specific type of company in exchange for its high effectiveness is an acceptable compromise. Looking at the wider business environment, 60 of the world’s 100 largest companies are from the US and fewer than 20 are European. And Chiness giants are growing faster than us. Why is Europe unable to produce global giants like Google or Anthropic ? One reason we are absent from these rankings is that rapid growth needed took place in the IT sector, where Europe simply fell asleep. Parts of our economy and politics remained stuck in the analogue era, and we did not realise how important this was. “Rapid growth needed took place in the IT sector, where Europe simply fell asleep.” And when high-quality IT know-how emerged in Europe, it moved to the US at a certain stage of growth. I see three reasons for this. What are those three reasons? First, the US has an incomparably larger financing market than the EU. Second, other legal environments are more certain. The US state Delaware has created the world’s best commercial legal system, under which most large US companies are incorporated. Not because of taxes, but because of legal certainty. Delaware has a commercial law system that no one can match. Read more MEPs back new EU‑wide ‘28th regime’ businesses plan — but fear a ‘European Delaware’ Third, non-EU markets have higher demands for new players. The US market is far more willing to buy products from young start-ups, while Europe prefers established suppliers. But I will add a caveat: a larger company does not mean a better company. Our weakness in the IT sector has cost us economic growth and created a dangerous technological dependency. The Draghi report warns of Europe’s strategic vulnerabilities in raw materials, chips and security. How should the EU respond to Chinese dominance in these fields? China has made good decisions and backed them with massive state aid for industrial sectors. This would not be possible in Europe. China also disregards ethical and environmental standards in extracting raw materials. But its technologies are of high quality. There are areas in which we can benefit from the fact that China has invested heavily and produces an excess supply of quality goods. Solar panels are one example. Cheap solar panels are helping us move towards achieving our climate goals. In critical sectors, we must use a combination of supportive and protective measures to build our own capacity or diversify suppliers. Where there are unfair state subsidies, we must impose duties to offset them, but not blanket protectionism, the cost of which consumers would bear in the form of higher prices for goods. Read more One supply scare pushed China into renewables. Two real crises still haven’t woken Europe up Chinese technology is also a threat… In terms of security, we must ask ourselves the extent to which there is a risk that China will use technology as a weapon, like [Russian president] Vladimir Putin does with gas. We must be careful not to use security arguments as a pretext for closing the market. We would deprive ourselves of competition that could bring down the prices of goods. If we neglect this, it also becomes a security risk. Czech EPP-group MEP Luděk Niedermayer (Source: Tomáš Benedikovič, Denník N) Is the growth of China’s electric-vehicle sector a threat to the automotive industry in Eastern Europe? I have the impression that this concern stems from the situation a few years ago. Dependence on batteries has gradually decreased thanks to dozens of new investments and research projects in the EU, although it remains significant. In 10 to 20 years, recycling will play a key role, reducing dependence on raw materials. European carmakers made a huge strategic mistake by suppressing the development of electric vehicles and promoting combustion engines. This article continues, but the full version is available only to EUobserver.com subscribers. Visit account.euobserver.com/membership

noticias.titulo: Listen: What do France’s centre-right candidates want for Europe?
noticias.resumen: In the race for the French presidential election, there are already four names on the centre-right: Gabriel Attal, Bruno Retailleau, David Lisnard and Édouard Philippe. For now, they haven't reached an agreement to join forces and put forward a single candidate.
noticias.texto: Production: By Europod , in co-production with Sphera Network . EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms . Find the full transcript below : In the race for the French presidential election, there are already four names on the centre-right: Gabriel Attal, Bruno Retailleau, David Lisnard and Édouard Philippe. For now, they haven’t reached an agreement to join forces and put forward a single candidate. But do they share the same vision of Europe? None of these candidates question France’s membership of the European Union, or the fundamental rules governing it. Nor do they call for changes to the EU treaties, unlike some other candidates. The differences are more about how critical they are of the EU’s current functioning. For example, both David Lisnard and Bruno Retailleau believe the European Commission sometimes goes beyond its original remit. Retailleau wants to make it possible to bring cases before the Court of Justice of the European Union when the commission is accused of overstepping its powers. Lisnard, meanwhile, wants to strengthen the role of the Council and the European Parliament, which he considers more legitimate institutions. Read more What Marine Le Pen and Alice Weidel are planning for Brussels He also takes a particularly strong stance on national sovereignty. He opposes situations in which EU law prevents member states from taking certain decisions. When that happens, he believes the question should be put to the people through a referendum. As for the biggest issue of the moment, the EU’s multiannual budget, none of the four candidates has set out a clear position on the size of the EU budget, or on how much France should contribute to it. This is quite different from Marine Le Pen’s pledge to halve France’s contribution to the EU budget. You won’t find anything of the sort in the centre-right candidates’ programmes. Édouard Philippe puts considerable emphasis on mobilising private investment to finance innovation. That’s a position often associated with the more fiscally conservative EU member states: rather than injecting more public money into the economy, they want to make better use of private savings. Gabriel Attal takes a somewhat different approach. For example, he proposes a common European artificial intelligence policy, backed by its own dedicated budget, much like the Common Agricultural Policy. Read more Europe’s youth take to the streets as the post‑war promise of a better life breaks down And he explicitly suggests that this could be financed through common European borrowing. Speaking of the Common Agricultural Policy, do they agree on what should happen to EU farming subsidies? Very much so. All four candidates place considerable importance on the CAP and want to protect France’s share of the funding. That’s hardly surprising: France is one of the biggest beneficiaries of the Common Agricultural Policy, which provides substantial financial support to French farmers. When it comes to agriculture, there’s one proposal from Bruno Retailleau that stands out: he doesn’t want Ukraine to join the EU’s agricultural market. This isn’t particularly surprising, actually. Many Europeans share this view, especially in countries where agriculture plays a major role. But unlike Retailleau, the other centre-right candidates don’t openly state this position. And what about Ukraine more broadly? Do they have clear positions on the war and European support? All in all, yes, although they don’t go into much detail. Their programmes are almost silent on this issue. Read more Europe’s centre parties are collapsing – and, for the first time, the far-right are collaborating, rather than fighting However, their public statements are clear: all four have consistently supported Ukraine, including through weapons deliveries and the possible use of frozen Russian assets to finance the country’s reconstruction. They also agree on the need to strengthen Europe’s defence capabilities. One way to do this, they argue, is to give preference to European-made military equipment. In other words, European countries should prioritise buying weapons and defence systems from European manufacturers rather than relying on American suppliers. Gabriel Attal talks about this extensively, and Édouard Philippe also explicitly supports the idea. Attal goes a step further, proposing an investment fund specifically designed to support small and medium-sized businesses in the defence sector. So, while the four candidates don’t have identical programmes, their overall vision of Europe is relatively similar. The main differences lie in how they want to reform the EU institutions, finance common priorities and protect national sovereignty.

noticias.titulo: Only Stockholm, Helsinki and Copenhagen meet EU air pollution rules, as stricter enforcement looms
noticias.resumen: Apart from Copenhagen, Stockholm and Helsinki, no other major European city currently meets the revised EU limits for nitrogen dioxide and particulate matter - exposure to which caused a combined 216,000 excess deaths in 2023 alone.
noticias.texto: Only three cities are on track to reach EU pollution goals by the end of the year, a new study revealed on Tuesday (17 November), enforcing existing divisions between northern and south-eastern European cities. Copenhagen, Greater Stockholm and Greater Helsinki were the only major European cities or conurbations to have met new EU limits for pollution, while the vast majority of European cities are falling short of the new standards – expected to be transposed into member state law by December 2026. Despite progress noted across bustling cities such as Paris, Stuttgart, and Oslo, the Clean Cities report found no other major European city to currently meet the revised EU limits for nitrogen dioxide and particulate matter, exposure to which caused a combined 216,000 excess deaths in 2023 alone. Clean Cities , a coalition of 150 NGOs and grassroots groups, found reductions in pollutants to mostly in cities that had implemented clean transport measures such as low-emission zones and electric buses, as well as changes in residential heating, improved cycling routes and school streets. Read more ‘Made in Europe’ and low-carbon rules up for debate as EU eyes industrial law deal “The strong air quality performance of the Helsinki metropolitan area is above all the result of decades of consistent, long-term efforts,” said Antti Wemberg, senior specialist at the Finnish ministry of environment. “The city of Helsinki has been proactive in communicating air quality issues and providing practical guidance on how individuals can improve air quality through their own everyday decisions and activities,” Wemberg told EUobserver. The European Environment agency found that 9 out of 10 Europeans are still exposed to air pollution at concentrations unsafe for human health, and this is largely concentrated in areas in south, east and central Europe. Tuesday’s study found the most polluted urban centres to be in Zagreb, Bucharest, and worst-of-all, Athens. noticias.titulo: ‘Forever chemicals’ lobbyists met EU Commission 37 times in push to escape ban ahead of key decision
noticias.resumen: As the European Chemicals Agency finalises its conclusions on so-called 'forever chemicals', a new report reveals regular contact between senior European Commission officials and industry lobbyists.
noticias.texto: The EU’s attempt to restrict so-called “forever chemicals” (PFAS) is facing a coordinated industry push for exemptions that could leave the ban badly weakened, a report revealed on Tuesday (17 November). The findings by the watchdog Corporate Europe Observatory ( CEO ) come as the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) prepares its final assessment of the proposed ban, the last scientific step before the dossier lands on the European Commission’s desk for a decision. The commission has signalled that it favours banning PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances) in some consumer products but may take a softer line on industrial uses, which it sees as vital to Europe’s competitiveness in sectors such as semiconductors, batteries and clean-tech manufacturing. With different parts of the industry each lobbying for their own exemptions or longer transition periods, campaigners fear the result could be a restriction full of loopholes. The fluoropolymer lobby, made up by companies and groups including Chemours, Daikin, Arkema and the trade association Plastics Europe, want fluoropolymers fully exempted from the PFAS ban. They say that they are essential to Europe’s green and digital transitions and that no viable alternatives exist. Since Ursula von der Leyen’s second term as commission president began, they have met the commission at least 37 times to discuss PFAS. That amounts to at least one meeting every third week, almost entirely with the most senior officials. But due to incomplete meeting records and vague descriptions of some meetings, the figure is likely to be higher, warned CEO. “It is a very damaging demand to make,” CEO researcher and campaigner Vicky Cann told EUobserver, referring to the full exemption. “It is very reckless, considering the health and environmental consequences of PFAS use”. Read more French kitchenware giant Tefal faces legal ultimatum over harmful chemicals, as Europeans’ health at stake A growing pollution crisis Over the past 10 years, the PFAS pollution crisis has got bigger. As its nickname implies, once created, they last forever in water, soil, and human bodies. This article continues, but the full version is available only to EUobserver.com subscribers.
